record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.original_question: For sample-splitting methods in observational study protocols, where data are randomly divided into a planning sample used to choose hypotheses, outcomes, or subgroups and an analysis sample used for confirmatory testing with appropriate multiplicity correction, how should researchers choose a good fraction of the data to allocate to the planning sample as a function of the total sample size?

evidence.quote: Examples of methods that control for the familywise multiple testing error rate are Bonferroni-Holm [56] or splitting in which the data is randomly divided into a planning sample and an analysis sample, hypotheses are chosen to test based on examining the planning sample and then the chosen hypotheses are tested on the analysis sample using Bonferroni-Holm with the number of hypotheses now being the number of chosen hypotheses from the planning sample [25, 117, 47].

In Section 5, we demonstrated that splitting may be a useful approach for selecting outcomes and subgroups in an observational study. Some problems that have not been well explored for the approach include (i) what is a good fraction for the planning sample based on the sample size?; (ii) how should we decide how many and which outcomes should be carried forward from the planning sample to test in the analysis sample?; and (iii) instead of just having one planning sample and one analysis sample, how can we use sequential analysis methods to allow for multiple possible planning samples before deciding on an analysis sample?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an observational study with a total of $n$ units, and suppose that the data are to be analyzed by a sample-splitting procedure: a random subset of size $n_P = \lfloor f \cdot n \rfloor$ (the "planning sample") is used to explore the data and select a collection of hypotheses, outcomes, and/or subgroups for confirmatory testing, while the remaining $n_A = n - n_P$ observations (the "analysis sample") are used to test the selected hypotheses with a familywise-error-rate–controlling procedure (e.g., Bonferroni–Holm) applied to the number of hypotheses chosen from the planning sample.

Determine a principled rule for choosing the planning-sample fraction $f = f(n) \in (0,1)$ as a function of the total sample size $n$ that optimizes the resulting confirmatory inference. Specifically, formulate a criterion (for instance, maximizing expected power of the analysis-sample test, or minimizing design sensitivity to unmeasured confounding under a Rosenbaum-style sensitivity model) and identify the value $f^*(n)$ that optimizes this criterion, including its asymptotic behavior as $n \to \infty$ and its dependence on relevant problem parameters (number of candidate hypotheses/outcomes, effect-size structure, and bias magnitude).
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work has begun to address this question. "Planning for gold: Hypothesis screening with split samples for valid powerful testing in matched observational studies" (arXiv:2406.00866, 2024) provides empirically recommended splitting fractions, and "Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies" (arXiv:2601.22782) proposes a numerical procedure for choosing an optimal split fraction adaptive to low- and high-dimensional outcome spaces. These results give practical and partial answers (e.g., small planning fractions such as around 15% often perform well), but a fully general theoretical rule giving $f^*(n)$ as a function of $n$ across all settings has not been established.

status_evidence.title: Planning for gold: Hypothesis screening with split samples for valid powerful testing in matched observational studies
status_evidence.snippet: The optimized split-sample method achieves an average of 92% of the power of a pre-analysis plan when employing an exploratory sample fraction of 15%.
status_evidence.claim: Provides empirically recommended planning-sample fractions with near-optimal performance.

status_evidence.title: Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies
status_evidence.snippet: A numerical solution was provided to determine the optimal sample split fraction... adaptive to both low and high dimensional outcomes space.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work provides a numerical method for optimal split-fraction selection, partially addressing the open problem.
